text: Motonori Matsuyama (松山 基範, Matsuyama Motonori; October 25, 1884 – January 27, 1958) was a Japanese geophysicist who, in the late 1920s, became the first to provide systematic evidence that the Earth's magnetic field had reversed in the early Pleistocene and to propose that long periods in the past existed with reversed polarity, after which the field changed to its current state. The era of reversed polarity preceding the present Brunhes Chron of normal polarity is now known as the Matuyama Reversed Chron, and the transition between them is referred to as the Brunhes–Matuyama or Matuyama-Brunhes reversal. Born in Uyeda (now Usa), Oita prefecture, Japan, on October 25, 1884, he was the son of Zen abbot Sumie (Sumiye) Tengai. His name was initially registered as Suehara Motonori after his mother’s family, Suehara Kou, and later changed to Sumie Motonori when his father became chief priest at a prominent Zen Buddhist temple in Yamaguchi. In 1910, he was adopted by the Matsuyama family, married their daughter Matsuyama Matsuye, and was thereafter known as Matsuyama Motonori. Around 1926, he altered the romanization of his adoptive family name to Matuyama in accordance with a new transliteration convention. He studied at the University of Hiroshima and Kyoto Imperial University, where he was appointed to a lectureship in 1913. After working from 1919 to 1921 at the University of Chicago with Thomas C. Chamberlin on ice, he returned to Japan and was made professor of theoretical geology at Kyoto Imperial University in 1922. He conducted a gravity survey of Japan from 1927 to 1932, extending it to Korea and Manchuria, and studied marine gravity using the Vening–Meinesz pendulum apparatus in a submarine. While earlier rocks had shown reversed polarities and the idea of past reversals had been proposed, Matsuyama was the first to conduct a disciplined study of the hypothesis. In 1926 he began collecting basalt specimens in Manchuria and Japan, and in 1929 published a paper demonstrating a clear correlation between magnetic polarity and stratigraphic position, stating that the Earth's field had been reversed in the early Pleistocene and older, and later returned to present polarity. This reversed polarity, especially as observed in ocean floor rocks, provided crucial evidence for Harry H. Hess's sea floor spreading hypothesis. He served as dean of the Faculty of Science at Kyoto Imperial University from June 1936 to December 1937, retired from teaching in 1944, and was made professor emeritus in 1946. In May 1949, he was appointed founding president of Yamaguchi University (note: the university transliterated his name as Matsuyama). In 1950, he was elected a fellow of the Japan Academy. Martin J. Head noted that Matsuyama was the first to document clearly from basalts in the Genbudō (basalt caves) in Japan the reversed magnetic polarity interval from 2.58 to 0.773 million years ago, now called the Matuyama Reversed Polarity Chron. The transition around 0.78 million years ago to normal polarity is the Brunhes–Matuyama or Matuyama–Brunhes reversal. At the 1973 Burg Wartenstein Symposium, it was recommended that the beginning of the Middle Pleistocene should coincide with or be closely linked to the boundary between the Matuyama Reversed Epoch and the Brunhes Normal Epoch, a definition finalized in 2020 by the Executive Committee of the International Union of Geological Sciences, which ratified the Global Boundary Stratotype Section and Point (GSSP) defining the base of the Chibanian Stage and Middle Pleistocene Subseries at the Chiba section, Japan, using the Matuyama–Brunhes reversal as a marker. The boundary around 2.58 million years ago between the Gauss Normal Chron and the Matuyama Reversed Chron is known as the Gauss–Matuyama reversal. Rocks in Crystal Sound, Antarctica, known as Matsuyama Rocks, are named in his honor for his work on ice crystals.
